questions.question: Your team docs are out of date: setup steps are missing, screenshots are old, and nobody trusts the runbook. A teammate suggests letting a model rewrite everything unsupervised. What should worry you first?
options: Confident-sounding instructions could be wrong or unverified and cause real failures when followed
The rewritten docs would use complete sentences that take too long to read
The model would finish the rewrite too quickly for the team to celebrate it
Old screenshots look charming and should never be replaced at all
questions.explanation: Documentation failures cause real harm when people follow wrong steps. This lesson builds on that caution by showing how to plan documentation help with verification and ownership.

questions.question: For `Scenario("release note", "stale date and no verification step", signals=("no source link",), impact=3, uncertainty=3)`, how is the score assembled?
options: `9`, because only `impact + uncertainty` is used
A base of `9` plus two points for each matched signal, capped at 20
`20` automatically, because documentation scenarios always need a launch gate
The number of controls selected, because controls define the score
questions.explanation: `score_scenario` computes `impact * 2 + uncertainty`, which is 9 here, then adds `2 * len(signal_matches(scenario))` and applies `min(20, ...)`. The signal list and description can each contribute matches.

questions.question: Which priority does `priority_for(10)` assign to a documentation scenario?
options: `launch gate required`, because every stale document blocks release
`guided pilot`, because 10 is rounded up to the 11-point threshold
`team practice`, because scores from 7 through 10 use that band
`awareness only`, because anything below 16 is considered harmless
questions.explanation: The function checks the thresholds in descending order: 16, 11, then 7. A score of 10 is below 11 but at least 7, so it returns `team practice`.

questions.question: For `choose_category` with two matched documentation signals, which index is used to select from `CATEGORIES`?
options: `len(matches) - 1`, so two matches choose the first category
The index of the first matching signal in `SIGNALS`, regardless of impact
Always the last category, because multiple signals require a release note
`(len(matches) + impact + uncertainty) % len(CATEGORIES)`
questions.explanation: For nonempty matches, `choose_category` computes `(len(matches) + scenario.impact + scenario.uncertainty) % len(CATEGORIES)`. This keeps the category selection deterministic while incorporating the scenario's severity fields.

questions.question: Why does `recommend` include at least two controls even when no signal matches?
options: It always keeps a two-control minimum
The function duplicates the first control until the score reaches 16
A no-signal scenario is treated as a PII incident and receives all controls
The controls are unrelated to matches and are always the complete four-item list
questions.explanation: With zero matches, `1 + len(matches)` is 1, but the outer `max(2, ...)` raises the slice length to 2. The recommendation therefore starts with `source citation` and `owner approval`.

questions.question: What evidence does `build_plan` preserve in each returned row for an AI-generated runbook or ADR review?
options: Only the category label, because score and rationale are considered presentation details
The scenario name, category, score, priority, selected controls, and rationale
The full source document text and a model-generated citation URL
Only the original iterable position, so reviewers can reconstruct the score themselves
questions.explanation: Each row includes `scenario`, `category`, `score`, `priority`, `controls`, and `rationale`. The rows are then sorted by score, giving reviewers both the decision and the signals behind it.
